title: How do you use AI for gamedev? Does anybody use AI game dev for most of the coding of their game? What do you use it for?
author: LeeksAreSpinning
selftext:
What has stopped me sadly from making my game is my reluctance to learn / illiteracy with coding languages. I've spent more time trying Visual Scripting than trying to write code myself even.

I had put my "I'm gunna make my own game!" on pause for years now, while I persue other things, but with the rise of AI it's given me hope of being able to do it again...  
  
is anyone here using Unity3D and using AI and unity3d assets to make their game logic work? Does it work?

TBH I want to make a japanese RPG type of game, maybe like octopath travelers or something, or old ragnarok online style with 2D spirtes on a 3D background, with atmosphereric effects and all that.   


I know there's all these packs on asset store and other things that can help but once you get them I'm always stumped by the coded C# scripts and what to do next. There's "dialogue systems" "combat systems" and everything. I guess I'd need to paste those scripts into AI and ask AI to rewrite or add systems to them or something.

How are you guys using AI?

comments.author: sirpalee
comments.body:
There are lots of use cases, from coding assistance to agentic AI writing bits and refactoring code, summarizing papers, using AI-based search engines to have better results than Google, extending design documents from short notes, generating textures, 2D assets, voices, etc. It is an incredible force multiplier for a solo developer, not 10x, but more than 2x in my experience.

Coding assistance is excellent as long as you understand what's happening, and the AI is just taking the burden and boring tasks off your shoulders. If you don't know how to code, and you expect Claude to write the game for you 100% with minimal interaction from you - that's not going to work.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
For game logic, I somewhat understand how things work, however I have no idea on the coding side. I've done various basic tutorials but for some reason I just can't with code, visual scripting was easier (Managed to make a pong clone and almost finish a platformer prototype lol).   
I understand a game needs a dialogue system, saving system, garbage collection system, hit boxes, animation controller, etcs etcs

Do you think with AI coding, and combing with unity assets (which writes a lot of these for you, they have a whole dialogue systems on the asset store) I'd be able to hack together a pretty good working prototype?

I guess the only way to truly know is to try! I've just redownloaded unity and am trying out claude right now.

replies.author: sirpalee
replies.body: Sorry, it's hard for me to judge how difficult it would be for someone who is not experienced with coding. I'm pretty sure there are people who stream game development with AI, that would be another good thing for you to check out.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
Okay so I've decided I may as well learn how to code while making the game. I've been back and forth between "Should I use Unity, Should I use UE5" for a while now.

Was halfway through a blueprints tutorial on UE5 when it dawned on me "I wonder if this is actually harder than using C++ with AI assistance, isn't AI going to make blueprints obsolete?"  
  
Now I'm wondering, if learning to Code, would C++ be that big of a difference from C# especially with AI assistance in correcting/troubleshooting code now?

FWIW, it just seems like C++ has more syntax / more confusing names? like a few extra steps for everything... What do you think?

replies.author: sirpalee
replies.body: As a coder with 20+ years of C++ experience, I recommend using Unity and C#.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body: Haha, fair enough. I may go that route, only reason I considered UE5 was cause octopath traveler / Dragon quest III HD2D were made in it and it was kind of the style i wanted to go for, and there's some resources on how it was made. I'll have to look for unity3D examples of similar games, I'm sure there are some. C++ Definitely feels daunting to take on as a beginner lol

replies.author: sirpalee
replies.body:
Up to you, but recreating the style of octopath traveller or transferring the tutorials from UE to Unity shouldn't be difficult. Or just lookup an octopath traveller / unity tutorial.

In the end up to you, whatever you feel more comfortable with. If you prefer blueprints and the unreal experience go for that. You can do a lots in blueprints and you don't have to write everything in C++.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
so far I followed a beginner tutorial on blueprints, he had me do booleans / variables / arrays / enums / strings, basically teaching me basic concepts of programming with it then applying it in game, it's pretty fun but also very time consuming. I guess I'm always looking for a "shortcut" cause I know how long all this is going to take.

I think AI will continue to evolve and help programming, so I'm thinking github copilot with claude 3.7 inside visual studio referencing a unity gameproject with asset store systems like Playmaker, Dialogue System, tweener, and all that would probably save me a lot of time, as they are all c# scripts I can just have copilot reference and write functions / logic for, and do basic FSM stuff in playmaker  
  
I'm still researching while cleaning up hard drive space, A lot of games I like have been made in unity surprisingly, most of the AAA games were made in UE4/UE5 and it's graphics are way better and C++ is way more optimized. Genshin impact was in unity but they heavily customized the engine (I think I read they didn't use cinemachine / timeline, but made their own editor for making cutscenes because of how quickly it would lag from heavy scenes?) ?

  
Anyway I'm just rambling at this point, always been curious how coding and games work lol

comments.author: Leading_Result2934
comments.body: Claude 3.7 works best for AI coding

comments.author: lkewis
comments.body: Claude 3.5 a 3.7 is the best LLM for coding and understands Unity C# and HLSL very well. You will get a long way if you’re doing something common that will have a lot of GitHub examples seen during training. If your game systems become novel or complex, you will struggle only using an LLM and not knowing how to code. ‘Vive coding’ isn’t really here yet in my opinion, you’re better using LLMs to assist and teach you how to code at the same time, because you will always reach a point where you need to understand how the logic of your scripts works so you can bug fix without getting stuck in endless loops of an LLM gets lost.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
I've been back and forth between "Should I use Unity, Should I use UE5" for a while now.

Was halfway through a blueprints tutorial on UE5 when it dawned on me "I wonder if this is actually harder than using C++ with AI assistance, isn't AI going to make blueprints obsolete?"

I was going to go UE5 cause blueprints were easier and there were a few templates for the game I wanted to make, but honestly, I think C#, HLSL, and AI assistance in coding is probably way easier than visual scripting now right?

Do people still use playmaker FSM while using C# + AI? I guess a FSM and playmaker would still be useful, but blueprints is kinda just like connecting dots on traditional coding...

comments.author: grumpy-grouper
comments.body: Start your journey with "code monkey" on YouTube

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
"I want to make a japanese RPG type of game"

"my reluctance to learn / illiteracy with coding languages"

You gotta pick one. The JRPG is way too ambitious, especially if you can't code.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body: I want to make a open world online JRPG with procedural story / environment and action combat similar to FFXV but with FPS elements like fortnite and a pokemon collection system

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: That's what I say when I want to give an example of the most impossible first game to make.

replies.author: lnvisibleShadows
replies.body:
This is absurdly difficult, especially if coding is givng you trouble, you need to learn to make a game first, start ultra small, then cut the scope in half again. "RPG" is the hardest category of game to make, they're basically 10 games in one, you will struggle to deal with all these interconnected systems unless you've built each one individually. 

But honestly this is normal, everyone always over reaches (comically) when designing their first game, I also tried to do an open world rpg lol. Then reality sets in, but its all part of the learning process. :P A.I. isn't going to make this any easier it has its own learning curve just like coding, you're just trading the difficulty of learning coding (which can get you exactly what you want) for the difficulty of learning A.I. (which may or may not get you what you want and isn't well developed in this field yet.)

I'd say learn normal game development while keeping an eye on A.I., A.I. tools can help, like code assist and 3d model gen, but it wont do the "work" of putting it all together, yet. :P

comments.author: JedahVoulThur
comments.body:
I use AI for coding, but I already know how to code. I use it for creating specific functions, giving me ideas, improving the code or fixing issues.
At it's current stage, I'm not sure if it can do what you intend to, I tried all the bigger ones and they are amazing but still imperfect and if I didn't know how to code I'd become crazy haha 

Anyway, I recommend you to try RPG Maker for your project as it is an engine specifically designed to create the genre of games you want, that way you avoid having to purchase all these plugins for Unity you mentioned.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
Do you think the biggest hurdle would be just knowing how the C# scripts and the created functions i.e. Public object: Function; work together? If I can understand game logic the only hurdle would be getting the C# scripts and functions written properly maybe?   
I'm realizing it's not going to be as easy as I thought, but do you think I could get through it with referencing the unity C# documentation along with AI to help debug the code and just "learn along the way?"  
  
I've thought of rpgmaker but it just seems like I'd need 100s of scripts / plugins to get to a style I'd want that seems more easily done in unity or so, I could be wrong though, but it seems like it'd be more work to get a custom thing going?

comments.author: Ok-Protection-6612
comments.body: Downvote me if you want, but can't your game survive on spaghetti code if it's not like an MMORPG or something? Of course test it for bugs.

replies.author: LeeksAreSpinning
replies.body:
How so? Does a lot of messed up code not break the game too much? lol  
  
I don't think it'll be that hard either right? I mean, there's a whole "visual novel" or "dialogue" system, all I'd have to do is know which C# scripts control what, then ask AI to add functions to it or write new scripts, open them in visual studio maybe and if there's any errors I could ask AI to debug it lool

I think most important thing I need to understand is \*game logic\* and how each C# script / function created works together to create it. Which IMO is actually the hardest part.

Besides with AI, and the C# dictionary I could probably reference and troubleshoot things that arn't working and figure it out along the way... But the best I've done with C# is taking the old xbox XNA framework and coding C# in visual studio to draw images on a screen and control a tank with arrow keys and shoot a ball with spacebar LOOL

But for the more complex systems there's unity asset store again...

replies.author: Amiral_Crapaud
replies.body: Why not test your concept in RPG maker first? Superb platform to double check if the meat of your RPG (aka the dialogues & the intrigue) actually work to begin with. My 2 cents...

comments.body: Just start making a game if you want, you'll learn programming in the process.

comments.author: Bludgeonist
comments.body:
I'm essentially in the same boat. Love gaming, and have tried a bunch of times to create my own game but, I've always gone with Unreal since it had blueprints and coding makes my brain itch. 
With AI becoming far more competent at coding, eg Gemini 2.5 pro, I'm thinking this is definitely the time to dive back in. I'll echo the others here and say that personally, I think the best bet will be getting the AI to generate code for you, while it teaches you the basics. That's my plan anyway.
The game I want to build is a massive open world survival horror game, so I KNOW that's a bit out of reach until I understand how to connect the systems together, which I won't be able to do unless I understand at least SOME coding.
That said, AI is only getting better and more advanced, and new tools will likely integrate directly into the engines, and once that happens, they're exponentially more powerful.
Cheers mate, good luck on your journey
